title: Tsenacommacah to the Chancel at Gravesend: the Werowance's Daughter, the Hostage, and the Exhibit
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Tsenacommacah, the Country of Her Father

stops.name: Werowocomoco, the daughter born to Powhatan
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; no document of any kind records her birth year or her birthplace. The year is back-calculated from John Smith's inconsistent statements of her age (about ten in the 1608 True Relation, twelve or thirteen in the letter to Queen Anne) and from the van de Passe engraving of 1616, which gives her age as twenty-one. Month and day are placeholders. Werowocomoco is the conventional placement and is inference from where her father held court, not attestation.
stops.campa: Wahunsenacawh, whom the English will learn to call Powhatan, holds some thirty tribal groups along the tidal rivers of the Chesapeake. No line written while she lived says in what year, or in which of his towns, a daughter is born to him by a woman whose name no record preserves. He has many children by many wives; this one he keeps near him. She is given Matoaka for her private name and Amonute for another, and in the household they call her Pocahontas, the playful one.
suggested_refs: The excavated Werowocomoco site at Purtan Bay, Gloucester County, identified in 2003
William Strachey, Historie of Travaile into Virginia Britannia (manuscript c. 1612), on her names
sources: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The True Story of Pocahontas'
William Strachey, Historie of Travaile into Virginia Britannia (c. 1612, printed 1849)

stops.name: Werowocomoco, the girlhood nobody wrote down
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from Powhatan ethnography, not from any text about her; no contemporary writer places young Pocahontas at any named town. Date is an ordering device for the segment.
stops.campa: She grows into the work a Powhatan girl is raised to: the corn hills and the bean vines, tuckahoe root pulled from the marsh, water carried up from the landing, the long night dances of the towns. No English writer recorded where she slept as a child, and no Powhatan writer existed to do it. Henry Spelman, who lived among the Powhatan as a boy, reports that children were commonly raised in the mother's town rather than the father's, which would put her childhood somewhere other than her father's capital.
suggested_refs: Henry Spelman, Relation of Virginea (c. 1613), on Powhatan childrearing and maternal custody
sources: Helen C. Rountree, Pocahontas, Powhatan, Opechancanough: Three Indian Lives Changed by Jamestown (2005)

stops.name: Jamestown Island, the ships in her father's river
stops.date_confidence: attested for the landing itself; she is not present and the stop is placed here because the arrival happens inside her father's country and is reported to him within days
stops.campa: Three ships of the Virginia Company put a hundred and four men ashore on a marshy peninsula in the river the newcomers name the James, forty miles up from the Chesapeake. They build a triangular palisade of split logs. To Wahunsenacawh they are one more small and hungry group inside a country he governs, arriving with metal, guns, and no women; to themselves they are a plantation of the English nation. The news goes up the rivers within days, ahead of anything else. She is about eleven years old and a day's travel away.
suggested_refs: The reconstructed James Fort palisade line, Historic Jamestowne

stops.name: Werowocomoco, Smith brought before her father
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1607; the exact day is not recorded, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Captain John Smith, taken on the Chickahominy by a hunting party under Opechancanough, is carried from town to town and brought at last upriver to Werowocomoco. Powhatan receives him in a long house with two hundred men about him, seated on a bedstead of mats in a robe of raccoon skins. There is questioning, there is a great feast, and after some days the captive is sent back to the fort with an escort and instructions about guns and a grindstone. That much Smith writes down within months, in 1608, and prints in London.
suggested_refs: John Smith, A True Relation (London, 1608), the earliest printed account of the captivity
sources: John Smith, A True Relation of Such Occurrences and Accidents of Noate as Hath Hapned in Virginia (1608)

stops.name: Werowocomoco, the rescue as he tells it seventeen years later
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and contested; the scene appears first in Smith's Generall Historie (1624) and in his c. 1616 letter to Queen Anne, and is absent from his own 1608 account of the same days. Date is an ordering device inside the captivity, not an attested date for an event most historians doubt occurred as told.
stops.campa: In the Generall Historie, printed in London in 1624, the same days at Werowocomoco acquire a scene: two great stones dragged in, the captive's head laid on them, the clubs raised, and the king's dearest daughter flinging herself across him. Pocahontas has been dead seven years and Powhatan nine when the passage is first printed. Historians have argued ever since whether he embellished, invented, or failed to recognize an adoption rite being performed on him. Smith's own 1608 book, written months after the event, has no stones and no clubs in it.
stops.quote: Pocahontas the Kings dearest daughter, when no intreaty could prevaile, got his head in her armes, and laid her owne upon his to save him from death
stops.quote_source: John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia, New-England, and the Summer Isles (London, 1624)
suggested_refs: The contradiction between Smith's A True Relation (1608) and The Generall Historie (1624), the central evidentiary problem of her biography
sources: John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)
John Smith, letter to Queen Anne (c. 1616), printed within the Generall Historie
Helen C. Rountree, Pocahontas, Powhatan, Opechancanough (2005)

stops.name: James Fort, her name written into the language
stops.date_confidence: attested to the printed vocabulary in Smith's A Map of Virginia (1612), compiled across his whole Virginia stay; commonly and wrongly dated and placed to the December 1607 captivity. I could not reach a full transcription of the 1612 word-list in this pass, so the number of baskets in the quoted sentence is reported as the primary reading gives it but is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: Smith compiles a Powhatan vocabulary and prints it in A Map of Virginia in 1612: numbers, kinship words, the names of animals, and a handful of whole sentences built for the business of trade. In one of them her name stands as a common noun of the working day, a girl who can be sent for baskets and paid in beads. The sentence exists because a soldier wanted a phrasebook, not because anyone thought her worth recording. Two little baskets, and white beads to make her a chain.
stops.quote: Bid Pokahontas bring hither two little Baskets, and I will give her white beads to make her a chaine
stops.quote_source: John Smith, Powhatan vocabulary printed in A Map of Virginia (Oxford, 1612)
suggested_refs: The Powhatan word-list in A Map of Virginia (1612), the largest surviving sample of the language
sources: John Smith, A Map of Virginia (1612)
Smithsonian Magazine, 'The True Story of Pocahontas' (which prints a loose paraphrase of the same sentence)

segments.name: James Fort, the Years of Coming and Going

stops.name: James Fort, a child of ten among the English
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1608 by Smith's True Relation; month and day are ordering placeholders
stops.campa: Smith's True Relation, the first English book written out of Virginia, names her once: a child of tenne yeares old, who for feature, countenance, and proportion much exceeded any of the rest of her father's people. She comes to the fort on Powhatan's business, with attendants and in the company of grown men, a chief's daughter carrying out a chief's diplomacy. She takes part in an entertainment staged for the strangers, wheeling and shouting through the dust inside the palisade.
suggested_refs: John Smith, A True Relation (1608), the only description of her written before she was famous

stops.name: James Fort, the baskets of corn
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance across Smith's 1608 and 1624 accounts; the specific month is an ordering device
stops.campa: The fort cannot feed itself. Its men are gentlemen and artisans set down in a marsh, dying of bad water and fever, and what corn reaches them comes out of Powhatan towns in baskets that Powhatan chooses to send. Pocahontas walks in at the head of some of these parties. The English write it down as a child's affection for them. In her father's country it is tribute diplomacy, the measured feeding of a client he has not yet decided whether to keep alive. The women set the baskets down inside the palisade gate and wait to be paid in copper.
stops.quote: Pocahontas with her attendants brought him so much provision, that saved many of their lives that else for all this had starved with hunger
stops.quote_source: John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)
suggested_refs: Powhatan tribute economy and the corn trade of 1608, as reconstructed by Helen Rountree
sources: John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)
Helen C. Rountree, Pocahontas, Powhatan, Opechancanough (2005)

stops.name: James Fort, the captives given back
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1608 in the Encyclopedia Virginia chronology and in outline by Smith; the month is an ordering device
stops.campa: Powhatan holds English men taken in the woods; the English hold Powhatan men in irons at the fort. Through 1608 the two exchanges are worked out in a slow traffic of messengers going up and down the river, and Pocahontas is sent with more than one of them. She is twelve or thirteen years old. Smith records her arriving to ask for prisoners and being given them: her presence is her father's signature, and the release is made to her rather than to the men who came with her.
suggested_refs: Encyclopedia Virginia chronology, 1608 delegation for the release of Indigenous captives
sources: John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)

stops.name: Near Jamestown, the warning through the dark
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; reported only in Smith's later narrative, the letter to Queen Anne (c. 1616) and the Generall Historie (1624), with no contemporary corroboration. Date defaulted; the episode is placed in the winter of 1608-1609.
stops.campa: In the winter of 1608 into 1609 Smith goes upriver for corn with a hard hand, and relations break down toward open killing. Smith is the only source for what follows, and by the time he sets it down she is famous and she is dead. Years later he writes to Queen Anne that Powhatan meant to have him murdered at supper, and that the girl came alone through the woods at night to tell him so, weeping, and refused the beads he offered her because carrying them home would betray her.
stops.quote: the darke night could not affright her from comming through the irksome woods, and with watered eies gave me intelligence, with her best advice to escape his furie
stops.quote_source: John Smith, letter to Queen Anne (c. 1616), printed within The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)
suggested_refs: Smith's letter to Queen Anne, written to secure her a reception at court, and the source of most of the rescue material
sources: John Smith, letter to Queen Anne (c. 1616)
John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)

stops.name: James Fort, the gunpowder and the report of his death
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1609; the day of his sailing is not fixed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: A powder bag ignites in Smith's lap as he sleeps in a boat on the James, tearing flesh from his thigh and hip. He cannot be treated in Virginia. In October he sails for England and never returns to the Chesapeake. The English tell Pocahontas he is dead. It may have been convenient and it may have been what they believed; the record does not say which. That winter the colony eats its horses, its dogs, and finally its own dead, the first Anglo-Powhatan war opens, and she goes out of English writing for four years.
suggested_refs: The Starving Time at Jamestown, winter 1609-1610, and the opening of the First Anglo-Powhatan War
sources: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The True Story of Pocahontas'
John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)

segments.name: The Potomac and the Copper Kettle

stops.name: Passapatanzy, married to Kocoum
stops.date_confidence: attested only in Strachey's manuscript of c. 1612, one sentence, undated; the year 1610 is the conventional placement and the day and month are placeholders. The Patawomeck location is inference from where Argall found her in 1613. Note the village is in King George County, Virginia, not Stafford County as some accounts and the roadside marker imply.
stops.campa: William Strachey, secretary of the colony, writes in a manuscript nobody prints for another two hundred and thirty-seven years that Powhatan's daughter Pocahontas is now married to a private Captaine, a goodly young man, named Kocoum. It is one sentence, and it is the only glimpse of her in the years the English were not watching. Where they lived, whether there were children, how long it lasted, what sort of man he was: none of it is written anywhere. She is about fourteen.
suggested_refs: William Strachey, Historie of Travaile into Virginia Britannia, written c. 1612, unpublished until the Hakluyt Society edition of 1849
sources: William Strachey, Historie of Travaile into Virginia Britannia (c. 1612, printed 1849)

stops.name: Passapatanzy, the daughter the Patawomeck remember
stops.date_confidence: tradition, not document; modern Patawomeck oral genealogy, uncorroborated by any seventeenth-century source, which names no child of this marriage. Date is an ordering placeholder within the traditional window of c. 1611-1613.
stops.campa: The Patawomeck are Powhatan's tributaries at the edge of his authority and they trade with everyone. Their own tradition holds that Kocoum was killed, that a daughter of his by Pocahontas named Ka-Okee was raised among them, and that a line descends from her that is living on the Potomac now. No seventeenth-century document names Ka-Okee, and the tribe's genealogy is not a document and does not claim to be one. It is memory kept in families for four hundred years, in a country whose paper was kept entirely by the English. Whether Ka-Okee lived is a question the written record was never built to answer.
suggested_refs: Patawomeck tribal genealogy on the Ka-Okee line, recognized by the Commonwealth of Virginia in 2010
sources: Patawomeck oral tradition as recorded in modern tribal genealogy
Encyclopedia Virginia, treatment of the Kocoum marriage

stops.name: Passapatanzy, the copper kettle
stops.date_confidence: attested; Argall's own letter to Nicholas Hawes of June 1613 and Ralph Hamor's True Discourse (1615) agree on the transaction, though the precise day is given differently in different modern summaries
stops.campa: Captain Samuel Argall, trading up the Potomac in the spring of 1613, learns that Powhatan's daughter is among the Patawomeck and offers the weroance Japazaws a copper kettle for her. Japazaws and his wife coax her aboard Argall's ship to look at it; the woman weeps convincingly and is quieted with trinkets, and by the time Pocahontas understands that she has been sold the ship is already standing downriver. Ralph Hamor prints the whole transaction in London two years later, kettle and all.
suggested_refs: Samuel Argall, letter to Nicholas Hawes, June 1613
Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse of the Present Estate of Virginia (London, 1615)
sources: Samuel Argall, letter to Nicholas Hawes (1613)
Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse of the Present Estate of Virginia (1615)

segments.name: The Captivity, the Font, and the Marriage

stops.name: James Fort, held against her father
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1613 by Hamor; month is an ordering device following the April seizure
stops.campa: She is carried to Jamestown and held. She is about seventeen, and nothing survives in which she says what she thought of the arrangement. The English demand of Powhatan the return of seven Englishmen, the swords and muskets his men have taken, the tools, and a shipload of corn. He sends part of it and stops. Months pass, and the negotiation goes nowhere. The colony that once ate out of her father's baskets now holds his daughter as security against him, and each side waits for the other to give way first.
suggested_refs: Ralph Hamor's account of the ransom negotiation, A True Discourse (1615)
sources: Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse of the Present Estate of Virginia (1615)

stops.name: Henricus, the minister's house
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was moved to Henricus and instructed by Alexander Whitaker; the date of the move is not recorded and the month here is an ordering device
stops.campa: When the negotiation stalls she is moved fifty miles upriver to Henricus, the new palisaded town on the James, and placed in the household of Alexander Whitaker, a Cambridge-trained minister who came to Virginia to convert Indians. She is taught English letters, the catechism, and the doctrines of the Church of England. None of the surviving letters asks what a hostage in the house of her captors is free to refuse. Whitaker writes home that she is willing and apt.
suggested_refs: Alexander Whitaker's letter, printed in Hamor's A True Discourse (1615)
Henricus Historical Park, Chesterfield County, Virginia
sources: Alexander Whitaker, letter printed in Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse (1615)

stops.name: Henricus, the font
stops.date_confidence: no source consulted records a baptism date; the only firm bound is that it preceded the marriage of 5 April 1614, so the date is given as early 1614 with day and month defaulted. Henricus is the conventional location and is inference from where she was held, not attestation. Some accounts place the baptism in 1613.
stops.campa: She is baptized and takes the name Rebecca, and at the same ceremony her right name, Matoaka, is spoken publicly among the English for the first time. The Powhatan had kept it back from strangers deliberately, on the understanding that a name handed over gives its holder a grip on you. No account of the day survives from anyone with no stake in the colony. What survives is a promotional letter printed in London, reporting that she renounced publicly her country idolatry, written to show the Virginia Company's investors that their money is buying souls.
suggested_refs: John Gadsby Chapman's Baptism of Pocahontas, commissioned 1837 and installed 1840 in the United States Capitol Rotunda, a nineteenth-century composition of a scene no eyewitness depicted
sources: Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse of the Present Estate of Virginia (1615)

stops.name: Matchcot, what she says to her father
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1614 by Hamor, who was present; the day is not recorded. Coordinates are approximate: the site of Matchcot itself is not independently fixed, and the modern West Point area at the Pamunkey and Mattaponi confluence is used as the nearest documented point.
stops.campa: Sir Thomas Dale brings a hundred and fifty armed men up the Pamunkey with the hostage aboard, burning houses on the way, to force a settlement. At Matchcot the two sides shout across the water and shoot at each other. Pocahontas is put ashore and sends word that she wishes to see her father. Powhatan does not come. Hamor records that she told the messengers she would stay with the English, since her father valued her less than old swords, pieces, or axes. Two of her brothers come down to the shore and speak with her.
suggested_refs: Ralph Hamor's eyewitness narrative of the Matchcot confrontation, A True Discourse (1615)
sources: Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse of the Present Estate of Virginia (1615)

stops.name: Jamestown, the letter John Rolfe writes to Dale
stops.date_confidence: attested as a document of 1614, printed in Hamor (1615); it is undated in the printing and the day here is an ordering device placing it before the April marriage
stops.campa: John Rolfe, a widower of twenty-eight who buried a wife and an infant daughter on Bermuda, writes to the deputy governor for leave to marry her, and the letter is an agony of self-justification. He fears he is being worked on by the devil. He insists his motives are the good of the plantation, the honor of the country, the glory of God, and the conversion of an unbelieving creature. Hamor prints the letter in London the next year as proof of the colony's godliness. He calls her one whose education hath bin rude, her manners barbarous, her generation accursed.
stops.quote: no way led (so farre forth as mans weaknesse may permit) with the unbridled desire of carnall affection
stops.quote_source: John Rolfe, letter to Sir Thomas Dale (1614), printed in Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse (1615), p. 63
suggested_refs: Rolfe's marriage petition, printed in full by Hamor and the fullest surviving statement of an Englishman's reasoning about her
sources: John Rolfe, letter to Sir Thomas Dale (1614), in Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse (1615)

stops.name: Jamestown church, married to John Rolfe
stops.date_confidence: attested by Historic Jamestowne and corroborated by Hamor and Encyclopedia Virginia; the officiant, traditionally named as Richard Buck, is thinly documented
stops.campa: They are married in the church inside the palisade, a timber building with a chancel and a cedar communion table, on the fifth of April. Dale approves it. Powhatan approves it too and sends an uncle and two sons in his place; he does not come himself and never in his life sets foot in an English town. The bride wears English clothes. The war that has burned villages on both sides for five years stops with the ceremony and holds for eight years, and Virginians will call the interval the Peace of Pocahontas.
suggested_refs: The excavated foundations of the 1608 church at James Fort, Historic Jamestowne, site of the marriage

segments.name: Varina, the Peace and the Child

stops.name: Varina Farms, the household on the river
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, flagged and not resolved: the Varina location is widely repeated by Encyclopedia Virginia and National Park Service materials, but the place-name Varina is first documented only in 1632, after Rolfe's death, and at least one reference work calls the association a persistent nineteenth-century legend. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Tradition puts the Rolfe household across the James from Henricus, at a plantation called Varina, where John Rolfe grows the sweet Caribbean tobacco he has been experimenting with since 1612 and which is about to make Virginia solvent. Somewhere along that river she keeps house on a tobacco farm and is addressed as Lady Rebecca. The tradition may be wrong about the house. The name Varina is first documented in 1632, years after Rolfe is dead, and one strand of scholarship calls the whole association a nineteenth-century invention.
suggested_refs: Rolfe's Nicotiana tabacum experiments from 1612, the crop that founded the Virginia export economy
sources: Wikipedia, 'Varina, Virginia', which disputes the association

stops.name: Varina Farms, the son
stops.date_confidence: the day is given as 30 January 1615 at James Cittie, Virginia in the genealogical record, and Encyclopedia Virginia is the outlier in leaving a window running to 1617; the country is settled by his documented presence as an infant on the spring 1616 crossing, so the older claim that he may have been born in England is impossible. The birthplace inherits the unresolved Varina problem above.
stops.campa: A son is born and christened Thomas, on the thirtieth of January by the reckoning that has come down through his own descendants, in James City in Virginia. Encyclopedia Virginia declines to fix the date at all and leaves a window open as far as 1617. He is an infant in arms crossing the Atlantic the following spring, which settles the country if not the day. Through his daughter Jane a great many Virginians will later claim descent from her, some with paper and most without. He is her only documented child.
suggested_refs: The line from Thomas Rolfe to his daughter Jane, wife of Robert Bolling, the only English-documented descent
sources: Gary Boyd Roberts, on the documented Rolfe-Bolling descent

stops.name: Varina Farms, the second daughter refused
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1615 by Hamor, who carried the message himself; the exchange took place at Powhatan's town and she is not recorded as present, so the stop is pinned at her own household and dated only to order the segment
stops.campa: Dale sends Ralph Hamor upriver to Powhatan to ask for another daughter, a girl of about twelve, to be married to Dale himself, who has a wife living in England. Hamor goes and asks, and writes the errand down himself. Powhatan refuses. He says the child is already promised, that he will not sell off what is left of his children, and that one pledge is enough between them: he desires no further assurance of friendship than the one he has already given.
suggested_refs: Hamor's embassy of 1615 and Powhatan's refusal, A True Discourse (1615)
sources: Ralph Hamor, A True Discourse of the Present Estate of Virginia (1615)

segments.name: The Crossing and the Jacobean Court

stops.name: Jamestown, the sailing for England
stops.date_confidence: attested to spring 1616; the day of departure is not recorded and is defaulted
stops.campa: The Virginia Company pays for a voyage. Aboard go John Rolfe, Lady Rebecca, the infant Thomas, Sir Thomas Dale, and about a dozen Powhatan people. Argall commands the ship, the same officer who bought her off the Potomac three years before. The company means to show its investors and the court a converted princess and a pacified colony in one body. Among the passengers is the priest and councilor Uttamatomakkin, whom Powhatan sends with instructions to count the English and cut a notch in a stick for every man he sees.
suggested_refs: Virginia Company promotional strategy of 1616 and the exhibition of the Powhatan party in London

stops.name: Plymouth, the landfall
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, flagged: three sources give the arrival at Plymouth as 12 June 1616, while Encyclopedia Virginia's timeline gives September 1616. June is followed here because a September landfall is hard to square with an April sailing and because the Tomocomo material also begins the notched-stick count at Plymouth in June. Coordinates tightened to the Barbican and Sutton Harbour.
stops.campa: They come into Plymouth in June, into a harbor of fishing boats and Newfoundland traders under the grey bulk of the Hoe. Uttamatomakkin gives up his notched stick almost at once; there are more Englishmen on the quay than he has notches, and more still behind them. Then the party goes up the road to London, some two hundred miles overland by coach and horse, through a country of hedged fields and stone churches and villages older than anything standing in Virginia. She has never in her life been out of sight of tidewater.
suggested_refs: The Barbican and Sutton Harbour at Plymouth, the party's point of entry into England
sources: Encyclopedia Virginia, 'Pocahontas (d. 1617)', which dates the landing to September

stops.name: London, Lady Rebecca on show
stops.date_confidence: attested in general terms by Purchas and by Virginia Company promotional context; her lodgings and daily movements in London are not itemized in any surviving source, and the day here is an ordering device
stops.campa: London holds perhaps two hundred thousand people, more than the whole Powhatan paramountcy, and it is loud, filthy, and built of stone. She is lodged, dressed in a stiff bodice and a tall hat, and shown. Where she slept, how she spent her days, whom she talked with: almost none of it went on paper, because she is there as an exhibit and nobody asks an exhibit for its account. Samuel Purchas, who meets her, writes that she carried herself as the daughter of a king and did not gape at what was put in front of her.
suggested_refs: Samuel Purchas, Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes (1625), the only eyewitness description of her in London

stops.name: Heacham, the Rolfe family seat
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; local Norfolk memory holds that the party visited Heacham Hall in 1616, but no contemporary document secures an itinerary stop there and the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: Norfolk tradition takes the Rolfes north to Heacham, John Rolfe's family seat on the edge of the Wash, and remembers a mulberry planted in the grounds at the visit. No itinerary confirms it and no contemporary letter mentions the journey; the story is village memory, not record. The village has kept her regardless. Her figure stands on the village sign at the green, and a memorial to her is set in the parish church. Heacham Hall itself burned to the ground in 1941.
suggested_refs: The Pocahontas memorial in St Mary's Church, Heacham, and the village sign carrying her figure
sources: Local Norfolk tradition, uncorroborated by any 1616 document

stops.name: London, sitting for Simon van de Passe
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1616 by the engraving itself; the month of the sitting is not recorded and is an ordering device
stops.campa: Simon van de Passe, a young Dutch engraver working in London, cuts her portrait into a copper plate. She sits in a tall crowned hat, a broad lace ruff, an embroidered jacket, an ostrich fan in her right hand; the face is her own, high-cheekboned and level, and it looks straight out of the oval. It is the only portrait made from life, and every image of her made since descends from this plate. The Latin around it names her Matoaka alias Rebecca, daughter of the most powerful prince of the Powhatan empire of Virginia, and gives her age as twenty-one.
stops.quote: MATOAKA ALS REBECCA FILIA POTENTISS PRINC POWHATANI IMP VIRGINIAE
stops.quote_source: Latin inscription on Simon van de Passe's engraving, London, 1616 (National Portrait Gallery)
suggested_refs: Simon van de Passe, 'Matoaka als Rebecka', line engraving, 1616, National Portrait Gallery, London
sources: Simon van de Passe, engraving (1616), National Portrait Gallery collections

stops.name: Brentford, the lodgings out of the city
stops.date_confidence: attested that the family moved to Brentford during the England stay; the exact house is not documented and the month is an ordering device within the winter of 1616-1617
stops.campa: The London air is coal smoke and river stink, and the Powhatan party is sickening in it. Several of the people who crossed with her are dying that winter, in lodgings. Through the winter the Rolfes move out to Brentford, a village of a few hundred souls on the north bank of the Thames west of the city, where the Brent comes down into the river. Anyone in London who wants to see her now has to make the journey out to her. The exact house is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Encyclopedia Virginia on the Brentford residence, 'then a small village outside London'

stops.name: London House, the bishop's table
stops.date_confidence: attested by Purchas, who was John King's chaplain and present; Purchas dates the entertainment to 1617 and King held the see of London from 1611 to 1621. No address for the occasion survives beyond the Bishop of London's residence at London House in St Paul's Churchyard; the month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: John King, Bishop of London, receives her at London House in the churchyard of old St Paul's, whose spire had burned off fifty years earlier and was never put back. Samuel Purchas, the bishop's chaplain and the man who will print the account, is in the room. He records that the bishop entertained her with festival state and pomp beyond anything he had shown other ladies who came to that house. The bishop is the second man in the Church of England. She is twenty years old, and three years earlier she was a hostage on the James.
stops.quote_source: Samuel Purchas, Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes (1625 edition)
suggested_refs: London House, St Paul's Churchyard, residence of the Bishops of London until the Great Fire

stops.name: Whitehall Palace, the Twelfth Night masque
stops.date_confidence: attested; the performance date of The Vision of Delight is fixed at 6 January 1617 and contemporary court report places her and Uttamatomakkin in the audience, well seated. This is the most firmly documented single hour of her time in England.
stops.campa: On Twelfth Night the court gathers at Whitehall for Ben Jonson's The Vision of Delight, with machinery by Inigo Jones: a winter night that opens into a bower of spring, dancers coming down out of the scenery, the whole thing lit by hundreds of candles and gone by morning. James the First is there, and Anne of Denmark. Nothing records what she made of a machine that turns winter into a garden. Pocahontas and Uttamatomakkin are seated well, which a courtier thought worth writing down.
suggested_refs: Ben Jonson, The Vision of Delight, performed at Whitehall 6 January 1617, printed 1641
sources: Ben Jonson, The Vision of Delight (1617)
Camilla Townsend, Pocahontas and the Powhatan Dilemma (2004)

stops.name: Brentford, John Smith comes at last
stops.date_confidence: the encounter is treated by most historians as real; the date is not recorded and falls in the window between the Rolfes' move to Brentford and their departure in March 1617, so early 1617 rather than 1616. The speech itself is Smith's retrospective composition, printed in 1624, seven years after her death.
stops.campa: Smith has been back in England seven years and has not written to her once. He comes out to Brentford with company. She turns her face away and will not speak, and sits like that for two or three hours while they wait on her. Then she speaks. She calls him father, and tells him what she was told in Virginia, and what her own father sent Uttamatomakkin across the ocean to find out. It is the longest thing anyone ever recorded her saying. Every word of it is Smith's, set down in print in 1624, in a book arguing for his own importance.
stops.quote: Were you not afraid to come into my fathers Countrie, and caused feare in him and all his people (but mee) and feare you here I should call you father? I tell you then I will, and you shall call me childe, and so I will bee for ever and ever your Countrieman. They did tell us alwaies you were dead, and I knew no other till I came to Plimoth; yet Powhatan did command Uttamatomakkin to seeke you, and know the truth, because your Countriemen will lie much.
stops.quote_source: John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624), the Brentford reunion
suggested_refs: The Brentford reunion passage in the Generall Historie, the only extended speech attributed to her anywhere
sources: John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)

stops.name: The Thames off Gravesend, taken ill aboard
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1617 by Rolfe's own letter to Sir Edwin Sandys; the day of embarkation and the day she was put ashore are not recorded
stops.campa: In March the party boards for the return crossing and the ship works downriver on the ebb. Somewhere between London and the open estuary she becomes gravely ill. Rolfe has the ship put in at Gravesend, twenty-five miles down, the last town before the Thames widens into open water and the customary place where outbound passengers took their leave of England. Nobody records what she is suffering from. She is carried ashore. Thomas, not yet two years old, is sick as well.
suggested_refs: John Rolfe, letter to Sir Edwin Sandys, June 1617, in Kingsbury, Records of the Virginia Company of London, vol. III
sources: John Rolfe, letter to Sir Edwin Sandys (1617)

stops.name: Gravesend, her death ashore
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested; the day is not recorded and is placed here the day before the register's burial entry of 21 March. Cause of death is undetermined: pneumonia, tuberculosis, smallpox, and dysentery have all been proposed and none is confirmed by any surviving medical record. The quoted words are Rolfe's report and his syntax leaves it genuinely open whether he is reporting her speech or offering his own consolation.
stops.campa: She dies in a lodging at Gravesend, twenty or twenty-one years old, an ocean and a year and a half away from the rivers she was born on. Pneumonia, tuberculosis, smallpox, dysentery have all been proposed for her; there is no medical record and none of them can be shown. In June, writing to Sir Edwin Sandys of the Virginia Company, John Rolfe reports the death and adds a phrase that has been read ever since as her last words, though the sentence he wrote does not make clear whose words they were.
stops.quote: My wifes death is much lamented; my childe much desyred, when it is of better strength to endure so hard a passage, whose life greately extinguisheth the sorrow of her loss, saying all must die, but tis enough that her childe liueth.
stops.quote_source: John Rolfe to Sir Edwin Sandys, June 1617, in Susan Myra Kingsbury, ed., Records of the Virginia Company of London, vol. III, p. 71
suggested_refs: The widely circulated modernized paraphrase, 'all must die, tis enough that the child liveth', which is not the manuscript wording
sources: John Rolfe, letter to Sir Edwin Sandys (1617), in Kingsbury, Records of the Virginia Company, vol. III
Helen C. Rountree, Pocahontas, Powhatan, Opechancanough (2005)

stops.name: St George's Church, the chancel and the register
stops.date_confidence: attested by the parish burial register itself, entered as 21 March 1616 Old Style, that is 1616/17; the register is the only official English document recording her existence in her own right
stops.campa: She is buried inside the church, in the chancel, which is where a parish puts people of rank. The clerk enters her under her husband's name and gets it wrong, writing Thomas, which is her son's name, and spelling Rolfe with a W at the front of it. The year stands as 1616, because in England the year still turned on Lady Day in March. Four words into the entry the record of her burial is already inaccurate, and it is the most reliable document about her that exists.
stops.quote: 1616 - March 21. Rebecca Wrolfe, wyffe of Thomas Wrolfe, gent. A Virginia lady borne, was buried in the chauncel.
stops.quote_source: Burial register, St George's Church, Gravesend, as transcribed in Wyndham Robertson, Pocahontas, alias Matoaka, and her Descendants (Richmond, 1887), p. 29
suggested_refs: The St George's, Gravesend parish burial register, which survives the 1727 fire that destroyed the church
sources: St George's Church, Gravesend, parish burial register (21 March 1616/17)
Wyndham Robertson, Pocahontas, alias Matoaka, and her Descendants (1887)

stops.name: Gravesend, the child left behind
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline by Virginia Company correspondence and Rolfe's own letters; the day is an ordering device and the point at which Thomas was handed over is variously given as Gravesend or Plymouth
stops.campa: Thomas, sick, cannot be taken to sea. Rolfe gives him over to the care of Sir Lewis Stukley and sails for Virginia without wife or son; the boy passes to his uncle Henry Rolfe in London and is raised English. He will be a grown man when he crosses to Virginia, and he will petition the governor there for leave to visit his mother's kin. John Rolfe marries again in Virginia, holds office, and dies in 1622, the year a Powhatan offensive ends the peace his marriage began. Father and son never meet again.
suggested_refs: Thomas Rolfe's later petition to the governor of Virginia for leave to visit his Powhatan relatives
sources: Camilla Townsend, Pocahontas and the Powhatan Dilemma (2004)

stops.name: Werowocomoco, the scene printed in London
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication; the stop is pinned at the site the printed scene claims for itself, and the day and month are defaulted
stops.campa: Seven years after her death and sixteen after his own first book, Smith publishes the Generall Historie, and the rescue at the two stones appears in print for the first time. That is what England will remember. The story travels on through Robert Beverley, through the schoolbooks of the nineteenth century, into a fable about a girl who chose the newcomers over her own people. The town where it is supposed to have happened lay under Gloucester County farm fields until archaeologists identified Werowocomoco in 2003.
suggested_refs: The Werowocomoco archaeological site, identified 2003, now part of Colonial National Historical Park
sources: John Smith, The Generall Historie of Virginia (1624)
Helen C. Rountree, Pocahontas, Powhatan, Opechancanough (2005)

stops.name: St George's Church, the fire that lost the grave
stops.date_confidence: attested that the medieval church was destroyed by fire in 1727 and rebuilt under an Act of Parliament dated 7 May 1731; there is no source dispute about the fire year, and the occasional 1731 date refers to the rebuilding. The day and month of the fire are not recorded here.
stops.campa: The medieval church burns down. Parliament passes an act for its rebuilding and a new brick church in the Georgian manner goes up on the site, and in the course of that her grave, somewhere under the chancel floor, is lost. Nobody now knows where in the building she lies. The parish register survives the fire, and the register is the whole of the physical evidence that she was ever in the town. The stained glass given by the Colonial Dames of America comes later, and the memorial in the churchyard later still.
suggested_refs: The Act of Parliament of 7 May 1731 for the rebuilding of St George's, Gravesend

stops.name: Historic Jamestowne, the bronze on the island
stops.date_confidence: attested; contradiction flagged and resolved against the looser account. The statue was modeled around 1906 and shown at the Jamestown Exposition of 1907, which was held at Norfolk and not at Jamestown, then loaned to the Corcoran Gallery, and only dedicated on Jamestown Island on 3 June 1922. Sources that report a 1907 Jamestown installation are wrong.
stops.campa: William Ordway Partridge models her in bronze around 1906, a barefoot woman in a fringed dress with her hands open in front of her, and the statue is shown at the Jamestown Exposition of 1907, which is held at Norfolk and not at Jamestown at all. It goes afterward to the Corcoran Gallery in Washington. Only on the third of June 1922 is it set up on Jamestown Island itself, a few hundred yards from the church foundation where she was married. The same exposition produces a five-cent stamp carrying her face, engraved from van de Passe.
suggested_refs: The 1907 Jamestown Exposition five-cent stamp, usually cited as the first US postage stamp to honor a named Native American
sources: US Postal Service commemorative stamp records

stops.name: Varina Farms, the exception written into law
stops.date_confidence: attested for the statute; the Act was passed at Richmond, some ten miles down the James from this pin, and the stop is placed at her own household rather than at the capitol because the law is an artifact of her descent and not of anywhere she went
stops.campa: Virginia's Racial Integrity Act defines a white person as one with no trace whatever of any blood but Caucasian, and then writes in a carve-out: persons with one-sixteenth or less American Indian ancestry and no other non-Caucasian blood remain legally white. The exception exists because the First Families of Virginia claimed descent from her, through Thomas, through his daughter Jane, through the Bollings, and a one-drop law without it would have reclassified the state's own gentry. Lawyers call it the Pocahontas exception.
suggested_refs: Edith Bolling Wilson, First Lady 1915-1921, who traced her descent through Jane Rolfe and Robert Bolling
Legal-history scholarship on the 'Pocahontas exception' in the Racial Integrity Act

stops.name: St George's Church, the statue in the churchyard
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5 October 1958 for the dedication of the Gravesend replica; the story that Elizabeth II admired the Jamestown original on her 1957 visit is reported but not independently confirmed here
stops.campa: A bronze cast of the Jamestown statue is made and given by Virginia to Britain, and on the fifth of October 1958 it is unveiled in the churchyard at Gravesend, standing out over the ground where the medieval church stood. Elizabeth the Second had visited Jamestown the year before and admired the original. An American sculptor's idea of her, cast twice and shipped east, now stands over ground in which nobody can find her. She had come to this Kentish river town by being carried ashore off a ship she never meant to leave.
suggested_refs: The Partridge replica in St George's churchyard, Gravesend, dedicated 5 October 1958

stops.name: St George's Church, four hundred years
stops.date_confidence: the quatercentenary is arithmetic and the general pattern of commemoration is well reported, but I did not re-fetch a programme or news source for specific 2017 events in this pass, so the details of who came and what was held should be treated as unverified
stops.campa: Four centuries after the burial, Gravesend and the Virginia institutions mark the anniversary with services and exhibitions, and delegations from the Virginia tribes come: Pamunkey, Mattaponi, Patawomeck. A century of scholarship has by now taken the fable apart, and what it doubts first is the rescue. She was seized, converted, married, exhibited, and buried abroad, and she left behind not one written word of her own. The delegations stand in the churchyard. Nobody knows where in it she lies.
suggested_refs: The 2017 quatercentenary observances at Gravesend and in Virginia
sources: Dossier summary of the 2017 commemorations, not independently re-fetched
Camilla Townsend, Pocahontas and the Powhatan Dilemma (2004)
